newsitem.title: UK: UK business group rejects proposed labour reforms.
newsitem.headline: UK business group rejects proposed labour reforms.

text.p: Britain's top employers' organisation, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), on Wednesday criticised plans by the Conservative government to tighten curbs on strikes.
The CBI said the current framework of industrial relations law in Britain was sound, and there was no need for further major reform.

The government proposals, which go even further than the radical curbs on strike action introduced by former Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher, would allow unions to be sued if a strike caused "disproportionate or excessive effects."

"Looking at each of the government's proposals...it is not clear that they will help to resolve disputes, and they may lead to more uncertainty in the workplace," CBI director of human resources John Cridland told a news conference.
"CBI members do not believe that all the proposals should be taken forward, although the ideas on re-balloting union members during long disputes are worthy of further consideration."
The CBI's comments were a setback for the government as the employers group has traditionally been sympathetic to the Conservatives.

But CBI president Sir Colin Marshall denied the organisation was being disloyal to the government. "All we are doing is responding to the Green Paper and expressing the views of our members," he said.
Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang said earlier it was the government's job to provide a lead.
"As with our previous reforms, we are confident that the CBI will be convinced of the importance of our proposals by seeing them work," Lang said.
The disagreement over industrial relations is the latest in a series of rows between the Conservatives, who must call an election within the next three months, and top business people.

The government, which is lagging the opposition Labour party in opinion polls, is concerned at the growing rapport between top executives and the Labour party, which has adopted increasingly pro-business policies.
Last week, deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine launched a blistering attack on businessmen who produced a report backing many of Labour's economic policies.
The CBI stressed on Wednesday that it would remain apolitical in the run up to the election.

Labour's education and employment spokesman David Blunkett said the CBI's response to the proposed labour law changes showed how out of touch the government was with the real needs of British business.

"It also shows that Ian Lang's pre-election gimmick has failed. There is now a growing consensus on the need for a sensible approach to industrial relations building on the strengths of the workforce and fairness for the future."
Labour has said it would not repeal Conservative legislation curbing the powers of trade unions.
But it is committed to signing up for the European Union's Social Chapter, which standardises worker protection across the 15-nation bloc and is opposed by the Conservatives.
